title: Bayesian Fay-Herriot Area-Level Model
text:
Code
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(spdep)
library(INLA)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(scales)

base_path <- here::here("data")
domain_frame <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "msoa_year_domain_frame.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

msoa_boundaries <- st_read(
  file.path(base_path, "boundaries-msoa.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  rename(area_id = all_of("MSOA21CD")) |>
  filter(str_starts(.data$area_id, "W")) |>
  arrange(.data$area_id)
Area-level SAE starts from the direct estimates created in the previously. The Fay–Herriot model lets direct estimates for each area-time cell, an MSOA-year cell in this example, borrow strength from predictors and spatial and temporal structures to stabilise noisy estimates.

Before fitting the models, we create a consistent numeric index for each MSOA and survey year. INLA uses these indices to attach random effects to the correct area and period.
The FH specifications include two area-effect structures: an unstructured independent effect and a structured spatial effect. The spatial effect uses area_inla_id together with the adjacency graph. The independent effect uses a separate column, area_iid_id with the same indices so INLA treats the two area effects as separate model terms.


Code
area_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["area_id"]]))
time_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["time_id"]]))

area_index <- tibble(
  area_id = area_levels,
  area_inla_id = seq_along(area_levels),
  area_iid_id =seq_along(area_levels)
)

time_index <- tibble(
  time_id = time_levels,
  time_inla_id = seq_along(time_levels)
)


To include a spatial random effect, we also need an adjacency graph .adj as input. We use Queen contiguity, where two MSOAs are treated as neighbours if their boundaries touch at either an edge or a point.



Code
msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  arrange(.data$area_inla_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$area_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)


The missing or zero sampling variances need to be handled before the modelling data are assembled, because it controls how much weight each direct estimate receives in the FH model.

For area-time cells without a direct estimate or variance, we assign the maximum observed positive sampling variance, signalling high uncertainty. Their estimates will be mostly model predictions.
Because the outcome is binary (1 for walking daily, 0 otherwise), very small samples can produce a variance of 0 when all sampled respondents give the same response. We also assign these cells the maximum observed positive sampling variance.



Code
max_variance <- max(
  direct_walk$variance[direct_walk$variance > 0],
  na.rm = TRUE
)

direct_walk_model <- direct_walk |>
  mutate(
    adj_variance = case_when(
      is.na(.data$direct_estimate) ~ max_variance,
      is.na(.data$variance) ~ max_variance,
      .data$variance <= 1e-8 ~ max_variance,
      TRUE ~ .data$variance
    )
  )


Now, we assemble the modelling data for INLA by adding the area predictors and the numeric indices for the temporal and area effects.


Code
model_data <- direct_walk_model |>
  left_join(area_covariates, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(time_index, by = "time_id") |>
  arrange(.data$time_id, .data$area_inla_id)

title: Bayesian Fay-Herriot Area-Level Model
text:
2 Fit and evaluate models
Each model uses the direct estimate as the response. The sampling variance from the direct-estimation workbook is passed to INLA as known observation-level uncertainty, so cells with noisy direct estimates receive less weight.
We define these model specifications and fit each one to the direct estimates using INLA.








Model
Name
Specifications




M0
Baseline
Intercept plus independent area effect


M1
+Temporal
M0 plus temporal random walk


M2
+Core predictors
M1 plus population density and no-car households


M3
+All predictors
M2 plus economic activities (full-time students, semi-routine/routine occupation, WFH)


M4
+Spatial
M3 plus spatial structure among MSOA adjacency




m0_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid")

m1_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  1 +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m2_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m3_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  cov_share_work_from_home +
  cov_share_students +
  cov_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(area_iid_id, model = "iid") +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

m4_formula <- direct_estimate ~
  cov_population_density +
  cov_share_no_car_households +
  cov_share_work_from_home +
  cov_share_students +
  cov_share_routine_semiroutine +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  ) +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE)

model_formulas <- list(
  "M0 Baseline" = m0_formula,
  "M1 +Temporal" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Core predictors" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +All predictors" = m3_formula,
  "M4 +Spatial" = m4_formula
)

fit_fh_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_data,
    scale = 1 / model_data$adj_variance,
    control.family = list(
      hyper = list(
        prec = list(initial = 0, fixed = TRUE)
      )
    ),
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE)
  )
}

fh_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_fh_model)







Note



When configuring INLA to fit an area-level FH model, these arguments are required:

The scale argument passes the inverse sampling variance to INLA, so direct estimates with larger sampling variance contribute less to the likelihood.
The control.family block fixes the Gaussian residual precision because the observation-level uncertainty is already supplied by the direct estimate sampling variances.



Next, we collate fitted values for all FH model specifications into one results table.


Code
# Main frame to keep from model data
output_cols <- c(
  "area_id",
  "time_id",
  "msoa_name",
  "direct_estimate",
  "variance",
  "n"
)

model_output_frame <- select(model_data, all_of(output_cols))

# Extract fitted values from each model and bind them to the frame
fh_result_tables <- map2(
  fh_fits,
  names(fh_fits),
  function(fit, model_name) {
    fitted_values <- as_tibble(fit$summary.fitted.values)

    model_results <- bind_cols(model_output_frame, fitted_values)

    transmute(
      model_results,
      model = model_name,
      across(all_of(output_cols)),
      fh_estimate = .data$mean,
      fh_variance = .data$sd^2,
      fh_lower = .data[["0.025quant"]],
      fh_upper = .data[["0.975quant"]],
      fh_ci_width = .data[["0.975quant"]] - .data[["0.025quant"]]
    )
  }
)

# Stack model outputs and set display order
fh_results <- bind_rows(fh_result_tables)
fh_results <- mutate(
  fh_results,
  model = factor(.data$model, levels = names(model_formulas)
)
)

To compare the fitted models’ overall performance, we use WAIC or (Widely Applicable Information Criterion) as a first check. It is a global predictive-fit measure returned by INLA; lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity.


Code
model_waic <- imap_dfr(
  fh_fits,
  \(fit, model_name) {
    tibble(
      model = model_name,
      waic = fit$waic$waic,
      eff_params = fit$waic$p.eff
    )
  }
)

M4 has the lowest WAIC and M0 is clearly the weakest model, suggesting that the temporal term, area predictors, and spatial structure together give the best overall fit among the FH specifications.

title: Bayesian Fay-Herriot Area-Level Model
text:
3 Further diagnostics

3.1 Direct To Baseline Model
We start by comparing the direct estimates with M0, the baseline Fay-Herriot model with no area predictors, spatial structure, or temporal structure to understand how the FH models fundamentally handle noisy direct estimates.


Code
fh_wide <- fh_results |>
  # One row per area-time cell, with model outputs in separate columns.
  select(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    model,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    fh_estimate,
    fh_variance
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = model,
    values_from = c(fh_estimate, fh_variance),
    names_sep = "__"
  )

direct_to_m0 <- fh_wide |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    direct_variance = variance,
    variance_change = .data[["fh_variance__M0 Baseline"]] - .data$variance
  )

wave_years <- sort(unique(fh_wide$time_id))







Area-time cells with high sampling variance contain less reliable local information, so M0 pulls them more strongly toward its baseline prediction. The Bayesian FH fit also produces posterior estimates for cells with missing direct estimates or zero/missing variance, allowing sparse or unsampled area-time cells to remain in the output with explicit uncertainty.


Code
fh_wide |>
  filter(is.na(.data$direct_estimate) | is.na(.data$variance)) |>
  transmute(
    `MSOA` = .data$area_id,
    `Wave year` = .data$time_id,
    `Direct estimate` = share_label(.data$direct_estimate),
    `Sampling variance` = round(.data$variance, 6),
    `M0 estimate` = share_label(.data[["fh_estimate__M0 Baseline"]]),
    `M0 posterior variance` = round(
      .data[["fh_variance__M0 Baseline"]],
      6
    )
  )

3.2 Adding Predictors
After the WAIC comparison, we inspect local estimate changes to see where the model moves the target estimates and whether those movements are substantively plausible. In Fay-Herriot SAE, adding predictors changes the expected value for each area-time cell, and unstable direct estimates are pulled more strongly toward those updated model predictions when the predictors are relevant.
For example, moving from M2 to M3 adds the occupation and work-pattern predictors. We map where M3 changes the estimates relative to M2, then summarise the predictor profiles of the areas with the largest upward and downward shifts (top and bottom 10%).







Code
m2_to_m3_drivers <- model_data |>
  select(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    work_from_home = cov_share_work_from_home,
    students = cov_share_students,
    routine_semiroutine = cov_share_routine_semiroutine
  ) |>
  left_join(m2_to_m3, by = c("area_id", "time_id")) |>
  mutate(
    change_group = case_when(
      estimate_change >= quantile(estimate_change, 0.9, na.rm = TRUE) ~
        "Raised most by M3",
      estimate_change <= quantile(estimate_change, 0.1, na.rm = TRUE) ~
        "Lowered most by M3",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  )

m2_to_m3_drivers |>
  filter(!is.na(.data$change_group)) |>
  group_by(.data$change_group) |>
  summarise(
    `Work from home` = mean(.data$work_from_home, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Students` = mean(.data$students, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Routine or semi-routine` = mean(.data$routine_semiroutine, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

The areas whose estimates are raised most by M3 have higher work-from-home and student shares, and lower routine/semi-routine occupation shares. This pattern is plausible: students and remote workers may have more flexible daily routines, shorter local trips, or lower car dependence, all of which could be associated with more walking for transport. The improvement in WAIC from M2 to M3 suggests that these added predictors also improve overall model fit.


3.3 Adding Temporal And Spatial Effects
The contribution of the temporal and spatial effects on the model prediction can be examined through two diagnostic outputs by INLA:

tau is the precision of the random effect, or the inverse of its variance. A higher tau means the random effect varies less.
phi is the BYM2 mixing parameter: it indicates how much of the area random effect is assigned to the structured spatial component versus the unstructured component. A value of 0.5 means the structured and unstructured components contribute roughly equally to the area random effect.



Code
fh_fits[["M4 +Spatial"]]$summary.hyperpar |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "parameter") |>
  filter(str_detect(.data$parameter, "time_inla_id|area_inla_id|Phi")) |>
  select(parameter, mean, sd, `0.025quant`, `0.5quant`, `0.975quant`) |>
  mutate(
    across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3))
  )

The temporal effect has a high tau than the spatial effect, indicating smaller differences between survey waves than between MSOAs. Meanwhile, the low spatial phi (less than 0.5) indicates that only a small share of the remaining between-area variation follows the spatial weights; most of it remains unstructured.
We can see where that structured spatial component affects the estimates by mapping the change from M3 to M4. In most areas the changes are small, with some clustered adjustments where neighbouring MSOAs share similar estimated walking rates, such as the more urban southern region.

title: Bayesian Fay-Herriot Area-Level Model
text:
4 Report estimates and uncertainty
Choosing the final model requires performance diagnostics, domain knowledge about the estimand, and enough metadata for downstream interpretation. Further benchmarking, such as comparison with related external indicators or sensitivity checks, can strengthen this decision when suitable data are available.
The final model estimates should be reported with their associated uncertainty. In the maps below, uncertainty is shown as the width of the posterior 95% credible interval. For transparency, the output should also retain the direct estimates, sample sizes, and direct-estimate variances.


Code
# Keep only the final, most structured model.
final_fh_results <- fh_results |>
  filter(.data$model == "M4 +Spatial") |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    msoa_name,
    time_id,
    n,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    fh_estimate,
    fh_variance,
    fh_lower,
    fh_upper,
    fh_ci_width
  )

title: A practical guide to Small Area Estimation for Urban Analytics
text:
Small area estimation for Urban Analytics

Urban researchers often want to use survey data at the scale where urban questions are asked: neighbourhoods, census blocks, transport zones, or other local units. This may involve comparing places, monitoring change over time, identifying local inequalities, or linking survey outcomes to area-level conditions. The problem is that most surveys are not designed to support reliable estimates at all geographic levels and time periods. When responses are broken down by area and year, some cells have only a few respondents and others have none.
This tutorial presents a workflow for choosing spatio-temporal Bayesian small-area estimation (SAE) methods for urban analytics. It focuses on method choice and shows how these approaches can be implemented in INLA.



Bayesian inference and INLA

Bayesian inference is used to combine survey evidence, auxiliary predictors, neighbouring-area structure, year-to-year structure, and uncertainty from sparse cells in one estimation framework. One advantage is that uncertainty of a modelled estimate is returned as posterior distributions for each estimate, which faciliates interpretation in policy contexts.
For code implementation, the examples are fitted with R-INLA, the R interface to Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation. INLA provides deterministic approximate Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian models, usually much faster than MCMC for this workflow.



Tutorial structure

The tutorial is selective. It covers the SAE methods most relevant to common Urban Analytics survey and auxiliary datasets, with the choice driven by outcome type, available survey information, auxiliary data, and population structure.


Estimation setup
Start by specifying the estimand: outcome, target population, areas, and time periods. This defines the area-time cells that need estimates and the inputs required for each possible route.
Direct estimation
Compute survey design-based estimates and sampling variances for observed area-time cells. If these estimates are precise enough and have adequate coverage, direct estimation may be sufficient.
Fay–Herriot area-level model
Use this route when direct estimates exist but are too noisy or incomplete, and the available auxiliary data are area-level predictors. The model smooths direct estimates across predictors, neighbouring areas, and time periods.
Battese–Harter–Fuller unit-level model
Use this route when survey microdata are available and the outcome can be modelled at respondent or household level. The fitted unit-level relationship is then aggregated to area-time estimates using area-level summaries of the predictors.
Multilevel Regression with Poststratification (MRP)
Use this route when population counts are available for poststratification cells, such as area by age by sex. The model predicts outcomes for each population cell and weights those predictions back to area-time estimates.




Tutorial data

The tutorial uses synthetic datasets based on the National Survey for Wales.
The maps and estimates illustrate the workflow and should not be interpreted as empirical findings for specific places in Wales. The synthetic dataset construction and preprocessing steps are described in the estimation setup step.



About the project

The tutorial is part of the TRACK-UK project by the City Modelling Lab.
TRACK-UK develops spatial and statistical methods for analysing mobility patterns at fine geographic scales and assessing their implications for transport decarbonisation in the UK. The project works with academic, policy, and industry partners to produce evidence for transport and energy policy.
For questions about the tutorial, contact:

Shaun Hoang - University College London
Anna Freni-Sterrantino - The Alan Turing Institute
Esra Suel - University College London; University of Zurich

title: Setting up for the estimation workflow
text: This workbook introduces the survey source, defines the estimand, documents the synthetic geography, and explains the analysis-ready datasets used by the estimation workflows that follow.

title: Setting up for the estimation workflow
text:
1 The Survey Microdata
The tutorial uses a synthetic teaching dataset based on the three survey waves of the National Survey for Wales (NSW) in 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025.
The NSW is a repeated cross-sectional survey of people in Wales, with annual survey periods covering topics such as transport, health, education, public services, housing, internet access, climate change, and the Welsh language. The cleaned microdata combine three survey periods into one harmonised survey microdata.
Since the survey responses are originally geo-indexed at the Local Authority level, but the practical tutorial estimates indicators at MSOA level, we use a synthetic MSOA assignment. The cleaned survey file keeps each respondent’s Local Authority and assigns a synthetic MSOA within that Local Authority using deterministic random allocation. As such, estimates produced from these data should not be read as substantive findings about individual MSOAs in Wales.
This design has two purposes:

Higher spatial resolution for tutorial purposes. Possible to demonstrate MSOA-level direct estimation, area-level SAE, spatial modelling, and MRP-style poststratification.
Privacy and disclosure protection. The assigned MSOA is not the respondent’s true MSOA, so we avoid presenting fine-grained respondent locations.







Note



From here on, the survey period labels are simplified to their end year. For example, the 2020-2021 survey wave is labelled as and referred to as the 2021 wave.

title: Setting up for the estimation workflow
text:
2 Data Preparation Pipeline



Preparation pipeline for analysis-ready inputs



2.1 Defining The Estimand
The estimand is the quantity we want to estimate. It should be defined before preparing the survey indicator or choosing a model, because it determines the outcome coding, denominator, target geography, time period, auxiliary predictors, and poststratification requirements.

Estimate what outcome among which population, across which geography and time period.

In spatio-temporal SAE, this estimand is evaluated for every combination of area and time period. Each combination is an area-time cell: one observation we want to estimate. In this worked example, one area-time cell is one MSOA in one survey wave year, or an MSOA-year cell.
In this tutorial, the estimand is:






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of Adults who walk for transport daily
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025






2.2 Preparing The Survey Indicator
Since we are interested in whether our respondents walk frequently as the main mode of transport, we can code the indicator from AtFrqWlk10, the active-travel frequency question for walking.

Use SampleTravelWeight in survey periods where this question was asked to a subsample and the weight for this exists,
Use SampleAdultWeight in survey periods where this question was asked to the main sample.

2.3 Preparing Auxiliary Data

2.3.1 Unit Predictors
Unit-level SAE, including MRP workflow, uses respondent-level predictors available in the survey microdata. We keep a small set of predictors that could explain frequent walking behaviour.
The unit-predictor output has one row per respondent-wave:

2.3.2 Area Predictors
SAE models sometimes call for area-level predictors that plausibly explain spatial differences in daily walking. The area predictors are drawn from Census 2021 bulk tables at MSOA level. The table keeps raw variables for interpretation and z-scored cov_* variables for modelling.

2.3.3 Poststratification Table
A population poststratification table is needed to apply the fitted estimation model to the target population. We built our poststratification tables from ONS MSOA quinary age-by-sex population estimates for the corresponding time periods, namely 2021, 2023, and 2025.

title: Multilevel Regression and Poststratification
text:
MRP extends the unit-level route by fitting a model to survey responses and then then averaging those predictions over a poststratification table that represents the target population in each area-time cell. This helps reduce bias from uneven sample composition in the original survey microdata.






Theory in brief



Let \(c\) index poststratification cells, such as age-by-sex cells within area \(j\) and time \(t\). A compact unit-level model is:
\[
y_{ijt} = \alpha + \varphi_{a_i} + \gamma_{s_i}
+ \mathbf{x}_{ijt}^{T}\boldsymbol{\beta} + u_j + \epsilon_{ijt},
\]
where \(\varphi_{a_i}\) and \(\gamma_{s_i}\) capture demographic structure, while \(u_j\) captures area-level variation. The area effect can be replaced by a structured spatial effect, and a temporal effect \(v_t\) can be added to represent wave-to-wave dependence. The model gives a predicted outcome for each area-time poststratification cell:
\[
\hat{\mu}_{jtc} = \widehat{\mathbb{E}}(Y \mid j,t,c).
\]
Area-time estimates are then poststratified using population counts \(N_{jtc}\):
\[
\hat{\mu}_{jt}^{\mathrm{MRP}} =
\frac{\sum_c N_{jtc}\hat{\mu}_{jtc}}
{\sum_c N_{jtc}}.
\]











Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of Adults who walk for transport daily
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025

title: Multilevel Regression and Poststratification
text:
1 Practical Implication
The current BHF page shows why a richer unit-level route is needed: modelling respondent outcomes without fully accounting for the target population structure can shift estimates away from the design-weighted Fay–Herriot results. MRP addresses this by making the aggregation step explicit, but it depends on having suitable adult population counts for the walking estimand.
